SCMP: "Nearly 70 per cent of the surveyed entrepreneurs said traditional manufacturing and service-sector firms were caught in a dilemma: companies had to engage in price wars to maintain revenue growth, but had to scale back operations if they wanted to preserve profits."

This, much more than ideology, is what has been driving the retreat of the private sector and the expansion of the public sector over the past two decades in China's economy.

In an environment of massive (and growing) excess capacity and pricing involution, businesses that operate under hard-budget constraints, and so need to preserve profits, must scale back operations. 

This requires that much of the politically-determined expansion in total capacity must be driven by businesses that don't operate under hard-budget constraints. As a result, manufacturing capacity shifts from the former to the latter.

This is an important point. When the economic value of a banking system's liabilities exceeds the economic value of its assets, the system can postpone adjustment only as long as it can capitalize and roll over the difference, in the form of accelerating debt growth.

Once it can no longer do so, however, the economy will be forced to recognize the underlying loss and – and this is politically the hard part – allocate it between households, different business sectors, and different government entities.

This could happen in the form of a financial crisis, and many times it does, but only in financial systems in which a severe mismatch between the structure and timing of assets and liabilities is faced with a sharp contraction in liabilities.

But in financial systems in which regulators are able to control net outflows from the financial system and to restructure liabilities at will – and China's is obviously such a financial system, just as Japan's was in the 1980s – the adjustment is unlikely to come in the form of a financial crisis or collapse. It is much more likely to be a long, drawn-out affair, much like what happened in Japan during the 2-3 decades after 1991.

Is this a good thing or a bad thing?

It depends. Financial crises can be much more disruptive socially and politically in the short term.

But because a slower, less violent adjustment slows down the capital reallocation process and generates deep and long-term financial distress costs (along with the associated hysteresis), it can be much more costly economically over the medium and long term.

So I would argue that the answer to the question of which is a better form of adjustment depends on whether the more important objective is short term political and social stability, or medium- and long-term economic growth.

If there is stagflation, the central bank is caught between two bad alternatives, so it typically tries to follow a monetary policy that compromises them.  Cutting rates can help support employment and the economy, but it also feeds inflation. The balance is delicate: too much easing fuels inflation, too much tightening deepens recession.
